The dispatch offers, as its first repair, that 'the `.cmd` can be run through `cmd.exe` with the arguments still passed as an array'. Measured, that is true only when the program element handed to `cmd.exe` is the BARE NAME. Handing `cmd.exe` the RESOLVED path breaks the array immediately: `C:\Program Files
odejs
ode.exe` is re-split at the space into `C:\Program` and `Files
odejs
ode.exe`. This fleet's own gcloud shim lives under `...\Cloud SDK\...`, so the resolved-path form is exactly the form that would have failed here. The shipped fix therefore resolves on PATH to DECIDE and passes the bare name to EXECUTE.
contradicted.two_theFailureKindCountIsNotWhatTheDispa: The dispatch's measurement table pairs `gcloud.cmd` with EINVAL and `gcloud` with ENOENT. Reproduced. Worth adding for the next reader: the legacy bare-name call in the SELF-TEST surfaces as `ENOENT` (the program name `npm` has no extension so Node never reaches the `.cmd`/`.bat` block), while a name WITH the shim extension surfaces as EINVAL. Both are spawn errors and both were previously rendered as `(exit ?)`, which is the point of the kind field.
contradicted.three_theVercelCLICannotReachItsAPIOnThi: `vercel whoami` SPAWNED correctly -- it printed `Vercel CLI 54.20.1 (Node.js 24.11.1)` -- and then exited 1 with `unable to verify the first certificate`. That is this host's TLS interception, not a spawn failure, and the mechanism reported it as `kind=exit` rather than as a spawn error, which is the taxonomy working. It is recorded because `served-commit-parity.mjs`'s console leg shells `vercel ls <project> --format=json` and will hit the same wall here, and because that repo's own suite already contains a test named for exactly this case ('console side REFUSES when the CLI fails, and names the TLS remedy only for a cert failure'). A reader who sees that red must not read it as this defect returning.
contradicted.four_theDispatchsEgressNoteIsNotReproduc: The dispatch's table shows `execFileSync("gcloud", ["--version"], {shell:true})` succeeding. It does, and it is the reason `{shell:true}` is the tempting answer -- hence the header's explicit refusal of it. Recorded so the refusal does not read as a claim that the one-word fix does not work; it works, and that is the danger.
